description: Introduction to Physics - Latent Heat - Calculations - Q1 (updated to LibreTexts version)
qtext:
Follow this tutorial to figure out how much ice is needed to cool lukewarm water to "ice-cold" temperature.

  1. Suppose you have a cup (about 250 grams, or $mass kg) of lukewarm water at $temp°C. Given that the specific heat of water is $cwater J/kg·°C, how much heat energy do you need to remove to cool this water to 0°C?

    $hintlink[0]

    You need to remove $answerbox[0] J of heat energy to cool this water to 0°C.

  2. Given that latent heat of fusion of water is $lfwater J/kg, how much ice needs to melt, in order to cool down the water to 0°C?

    $hintlink[1]

    About $answerbox[1] kg of ice is needed to produce a mixture that is water at 0°C.

What above calculation shows is that, for most range of water temperatures (from the reasonably cold 10°C to rather warm 40°C), 1:1 ratio of ice-to-water mixture will provide enough ice to cool down the water to the ice-cold temperature, and there will still be some ice left to keep the ice-water cold for some time.
control:
$anstypes=array("number","number")
$reltolerance=0.01

$temp=rrand(25,40,1) // lukewarm temperature in deg C
$mass=0.25 // mass of water in kg
$cwater=4186 // water specific heat in J/kg*degC
$lfwater=334000 // water latent heat of fusion in J/kg

$answer[0]=$cwater*$mass*$temp // heat needing to be removed
$answer[1]=$answer[0]/$lfwater // kilograms of ice needed

$hinttext[0]="Look carefully at the units of specific heat of water. It gives amount of energy needed (joules) per mass (kilogram) per temperature change (°C). What do you need to do to this number to get the amount of energy?"
$hintlink[0]=forminlinebutton("Hint (a)",$hinttext[0])

$hinttext[1]="You have the amount of heat energy you need to absorb from part (a) above. Look carefully at the unit of latent heat of fusion, amount of energy (joule) per mass (kilogram). How can you combine this with the amount of energy to end up with a unit of mass (kilogram)?"

description: Introduction to Physics - Thermodynamics - Efficiency - Q2 (updated to LibreTexts version)
qtext:
Carnot efficiency—theoretical maximum efficiency—can be calculated with just the temperatures of the thermal reservoirs. This makes it a useful tool to quickly estimate possible efficiency for different situations. Try the calculations below.

$hintlink[0]

  1. Automobile fuel ignites at about $auto K. Estimate the Carnot efficiency assuming that this is the temperature of high-temperature thermal reservoir and the low-temperature thermal reservoir is at the approximate room temperature $room K.

    The Carnot efficiency for automobile engines is $answerbox[0]%.

  2. In a steam-electric power station, fossil-fuel powered superheater provides steam of high temperature $steam K. Estimate the Carnot efficiency assuming that the temperature of low-temperature reservoir is at about $cond K (temperature of the condenser kept well below 100°C).

    The Carnot efficiency for steam-electric power station is $answerbox[1]%.

  3. A lecture-demonstration Stirling engine uses a hot cup of coffee as the source of heat energy. Using $coffee K (the coffee temperature) as the temperature of the high-temperature reservoir and $room K (room temperature) as the low-temperature reservoir, estimate the Carnot efficiency.

description: Introduction to Physics (Essay Questions) - Thermal Physics - Heat Engine Efficiency
qtext:
One of the surprising things you learn about heat engines is how inefficient they are, even when you imagine an ideal heat engine. Explain why heat engines are inefficient and describe the consequence of their inefficiency. Make sure to address: (i) definition of efficiency, (ii) the reason even ideal heat engines can never be 100% efficient, and (iii) how inefficiency of heat engine relates to the fact that you cannot cool your kitchen by leaving the refrigerator door open.

$answerbox
control: $showanswer="Efficiency is defined as `\"what you want\"/\"what you pay\"`. In the case of heat engine, `\"what you want\"` is mechanical work done (`W`), and `\"what you pay\"` is the heat input (`Q_h`). So, efficiency of heat engine is `W/Q_h`. Since heat engines expel some heat (`Q_c`) during each cycle to make net entropy change equal to zero, `Q_h` is greater than `W` (from First Law, `W=Q_h-Q_c`), and efficiency is less than 1, that is, 100%. This also applies to refrigerators (and heat pumps), which can be thought of as heat engine cycles run backward, with work input being equal to `Q_h-Q_c`. Since refrigerator expels heat amount equal to `Q=W+Q_c` (i.e. equal to `Q_h`), after having taken in heat of `Q_c` from its colder interior, looking at the kitchen as a whole, the refrigerator adds net heat of `W` (that is, it turns mechanical work input into heat overall)."

description: Introduction to Physics (Essay Questions) - Thermal Physics - Refrigerators and Second Law
qtext:
Explain briefly how a refrigerator transfers heat from cold object (inside of the refrigerator) to the hotter object (outside of the object). Explain in addition: (i) why doesn't this violate the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and (ii) why can't this be used to cool your kitchen?

$answerbox
control:
$showanswer="

Refrigerator transfers heat by going through heat engine processes in reverse. By doing mechanical work (provided by the compressor of the refrigerator), it \"pumps\" heat from low temperature to high temperature. (i) This is consistent with the Second Law of Thermodynamics because heat is not flowing spontaneously from cold to hot (process requires work input), and (ii) this cannot cool the kitchen because, on net, thermal energy increases, as the mechanical work input is turned into heat.

Additional Not-So-Brief Detail/Note: Compressor makes this possible this way: by compressing or expanding the refrigerant fluid, you can change its temperature (this is from First Law). So compressor compresses the fluid outside (making it hotter than the outside temperature, so that heat spontaneously flows from the refrigerant fluid to the outside), and it lets the fluid expand inside, making it colder so that heat will again spontaneously flow from the inside to the colder refrigerant fluid. (So, although on net heat flows from cold to hot in this process, in each individual heat-transferring step, heat is always spontaneously flowing from hot to cold, consistent with the Second Law.)

"
